claim: Type 2 diabetes accounts for approximately 90% of all cases of diabetes.
source: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) accounts for ~90% of all cases of diabetes, resulting in an estimated 6.7 million deaths in 2021, according to the International Diabetes Federation.
evidence: Cited to the International Diabetes Federation as the source of this statistic.

claim: Type 2 diabetes resulted in an estimated 6.7 million deaths in 2021.
source: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) accounts for ~90% of all cases of diabetes, resulting in an estimated 6.7 million deaths in 2021, according to the International Diabetes Federation.
evidence: Cited to the International Diabetes Federation as the source of this statistic.

claim: Early detection of patients with high risk of developing T2D can reduce the incidence of the disease through a change in lifestyle, diet, or medication.
source: Early detection of patients with high risk of developing T2D can reduce the incidence of the disease through a change in lifestyle, diet, or medication.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established medical knowledge and is later supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Populations of lower socio-demographic status are more susceptible to T2D and might have limited resources or access to sophisticated computational resources.
source: Since populations of lower socio-demographic status are more susceptible to T2D and might have limited resources or access to sophisticated computational resources, there is a need for accurate yet accessible prediction models.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about health disparities and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The study analyzed data from 44,709 nondiabetic UK Biobank participants aged 40–69.
source: In this study, we analyzed data from 44,709 nondiabetic UK Biobank participants aged 40–69, predicting the risk of T2D onset within a selected time frame (mean of 7.3 years with an SD of 2.3 years).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study's cohort size and characteristics.

claim: The mean follow-up time for T2D onset prediction was 7.3 years with a standard deviation of 2.3 years.
source: In this study, we analyzed data from 44,709 nondiabetic UK Biobank participants aged 40–69, predicting the risk of T2D onset within a selected time frame (mean of 7.3 years with an SD of 2.3 years).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study's follow-up period.

claim: The study started with 798 features identified as potential predictors for T2D onset.
source: We started with 798 features that we identified as potential predictors for T2D onset.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the initial feature set used in the study.

claim: The nonlaboratory model uses sex, age, weight, height, waist size, hip circumference, waist-to-hip ratio, and body mass index as covariates.
source: We established the nonlaboratory model using the following covariates: sex, age, weight, height, waist size, hip circumference, waist-to-hip ratio, and body mass index.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the features used in the nonlaboratory model.

claim: The laboratory model uses age and sex together with four common blood tests: high-density lipoprotein (HDL), gamma-glutamyl transferase, glycated hemoglobin, and triglycerides.
source: For the laboratory model, we used age and sex together with four common blood tests: high-density lipoprotein (HDL), gamma-glutamyl transferase, glycated hemoglobin, and triglycerides.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the features used in the laboratory model.

claim: The nonlaboratory scorecard model achieved an area under the receiver operating curve (auROC) of 0.81 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.77–0.84).
source: The nonlaboratory scorecard model achieved an area under the receiver operating curve (auROC) of 0.81 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.77–0.84) and an odds ratio (OR) between the upper and fifth prevalence deciles of 17.2 (95% CI 5–66).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model's performance metric based on the study's data.

claim: The nonlaboratory scorecard model achieved an odds ratio between the upper and fifth prevalence deciles of 17.2 (95% CI 5–66).
source: The nonlaboratory scorecard model achieved an area under the receiver operating curve (auROC) of 0.81 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.77–0.84) and an odds ratio (OR) between the upper and fifth prevalence deciles of 17.2 (95% CI 5–66).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model's performance metric based on the study's data.

claim: Using the nonlaboratory model, three risk groups were classified with 1% (0.8–1%), 5% (3–6%), and 9% (7–12%) risk of developing T2D.
source: Using this model, we classified three risk groups, a group with 1% (0.8–1%), 5% (3–6%), and the third group with a 9% (7–12%) risk of developing T2D.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the risk stratification achieved by the model.

claim: The blood test scorecard model achieved an auROC of 0.87 (95% CI 0.85–0.90).
source: Using this model, we achieved an auROC of 0.87 (95% CI 0.85–0.90) and a deciles' OR of ×48 (95% CI 12–109).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model's performance metric based on the study's data.

claim: The blood test scorecard model achieved a deciles' OR of ×48 (95% CI 12–109).
source: Using this model, we achieved an auROC of 0.87 (95% CI 0.85–0.90) and a deciles' OR of ×48 (95% CI 12–109).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model's performance metric based on the study's data.

claim: Using the blood test model, the cohort was classified into four risk groups with risks of 0.5% (0.4–7%), 3% (2–4%), 10% (8–12%), and 23% (10–37%) of developing T2D.
source: Using this model, we classified the cohort into four risk groups with the following risks: 0.5% (0.4–7%); 3% (2–4%); 10% (8–12%); and a high-risk group of 23% (10–37%) of developing T2D.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the risk stratification achieved by the model.

claim: When applying the blood tests model using the external validation cohort (Clalit), an auROC of 0.75 (95% CI 0.74–0.75) was achieved.
source: When applying the blood tests model using the external validation cohort (Clalit), we achieved an auROC of 0.75 (95% CI 0.74–0.75).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model's performance on an external validation dataset.

claim: Additional comprehensive models including genotyping data and other environmental factors did not provide cost-efficient benefits over the four blood test model.
source: We analyzed several additional comprehensive models, which included genotyping data and other environmental factors. We found that these models did not provide cost-efficient benefits over the four blood test model.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the comparative analysis of different models.

claim: The German Diabetes Risk Score (GDRS) model, trained using the study's data, achieved an auROC of 0.73 (0.69–0.76).
source: The commonly used German Diabetes Risk Score (GDRS) and Finnish Diabetes Risk Score (FINDRISC) models, trained using our data, achieved an auROC of 0.73 (0.69–0.76) and 0.66 (0.62–0.70), respectively, inferior to the results achieved by the four blood test model and by the anthropometry models.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the GDRS model's performance when trained on the study's data.

claim: The Finnish Diabetes Risk Score (FINDRISC) model, trained using the study's data, achieved an auROC of 0.66 (0.62–0.70).
source: The commonly used German Diabetes Risk Score (GDRS) and Finnish Diabetes Risk Score (FINDRISC) models, trained using our data, achieved an auROC of 0.73 (0.69–0.76) and 0.66 (0.62–0.70), respectively, inferior to the results achieved by the four blood test model and by the anthropometry models.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the FINDRISC model's performance when trained on the study's data.

claim: The GDRS and FINDRISC models performed inferior to the four blood test model and the anthropometry models.
source: The commonly used German Diabetes Risk Score (GDRS) and Finnish Diabetes Risk Score (FINDRISC) models, trained using our data, achieved an auROC of 0.73 (0.69–0.76) and 0.66 (0.62–0.70), respectively, inferior to the results achieved by the four blood test model and by the anthropometry models.
evidence: This is a direct comparative statement based on the performance metrics obtained in the study.

claim: The prevalence of type 2 diabetes has increased from 4.7% in 1980 to 10% in 2021.
source: The prevalence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) has increased from 4.7% in 1980 to 10% in 2021, and is considered the cause of an estimated 6.7 million deaths in 2021 (International Diabetes Federation - Type 2 diabetes, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the International Diabetes Federation.

claim: T2D is characterized by insulin resistance, resulting in hyperglycemia.
source: T2D is characterized by insulin resistance, resulting in hyperglycemia, and accounts for ~90% of all diabetes cases (Zimmet et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In recent years, the prevalence of diabetes has been rising more rapidly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) than in high-income countries.
source: In recent years, the prevalence of diabetes has been rising more rapidly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) than in high-income countries (Diabetes programme, WHO, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the WHO Diabetes programme.

claim: In 2019, Eberhard et al. estimated that every second person with diabetes in the world is undiagnosed.
source: In 2019, Eberhard et al. estimated that every other person with diabetes in the world is undiagnosed (Standl et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Standl et al., 2019.

claim: 83.8% of all cases of undiagnosed diabetes are in low-mid-income countries.
source: 83.8% of all cases of undiagnosed diabetes are in low-mid-income countries (Beagley et al., 2014), and according to the IDF Diabetes Atlas, over 75% of adults with diabetes live in low- to middle-income countries (IDF Diabetes Atlas, 2022), where laboratory diagnostic testing is limited (Wilson et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Beagley et al., 2014.

claim: Over 75% of adults with diabetes live in low- to middle-income countries.
source: 83.8% of all cases of undiagnosed diabetes are in low-mid-income countries (Beagley et al., 2014), and according to the IDF Diabetes Atlas, over 75% of adults with diabetes live in low- to middle-income countries (IDF Diabetes Atlas, 2022), where laboratory diagnostic testing is limited (Wilson et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the IDF Diabetes Atlas, 2022.

claim: Laboratory diagnostic testing is limited in low- to middle-income countries.
source: 83.8% of all cases of undiagnosed diabetes are in low-mid-income countries (Beagley et al., 2014), and according to the IDF Diabetes Atlas, over 75% of adults with diabetes live in low- to middle-income countries (IDF Diabetes Atlas, 2022), where laboratory diagnostic testing is limited (Wilson et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2018.

claim: A healthy diet, regular physical activity, maintaining normal body weight, and avoiding tobacco use can prevent or delay T2D onset.
source: According to several studies, a healthy diet, regular physical activity, maintaining normal body weight, and avoiding tobacco use can prevent or delay T2D onset (Home, 2022; Diabetes programme, WHO, 2021; Knowler et al., 2002; Lindström et al., 2006; Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to studies on diabetes prevention.

claim: The FINDRISC is a commonly used, noninvasive T2D risk-score model that estimates the risk of patients between the ages of 35 and 64 of developing T2D within 10 years.
source: The Finnish Diabetes Risk Score (FINDRISC), a commonly used, noninvasive T2D risk-score model, estimates the risk of patients between the ages of 35 and 64 of developing T2D within 10 years.
evidence: This is a statement about an established clinical tool.

claim: The FINDRISC was created based on a prospective cohort of 4746 and 4615 individuals in Finland in 1987 and 1992, respectively.
source: The FINDRISC was created based on a prospective cohort of 4746 and 4615 individuals in Finland in 1987 and 1992, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement about the development of the FINDRISC model, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: The FINDRISC model employs gender, age, body mass index (BMI), blood pressure medications, a history of high blood glucose, physical activity, daily consumption of fruits, berries, or vegetables, and family history of diabetes as the parameters for the model.
source: The FINDRISC model employs gender, age, body mass index (BMI), blood pressure medications, a history of high blood glucose, physical activity, daily consumption of fruits, berries, or vegetables, and family history of diabetes as the parameters for the model.
evidence: This is a statement about the features used in the FINDRISC model.

claim: The German Diabetes Risk Score (GDRS) estimates the 5-year risk of developing T2D.
source: Another commonly used scorecard prediction model is the German Diabetes Risk Score (GDRS), which estimates the 5-year risk of developing T2D.
evidence: This is a statement about an established clinical tool.

claim: The GDRS is based on 9729 men and 15,438 women between the ages of 35–65 from the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC)-Potsdam study.
source: The GDRS is based on 9729 men and 15,438 women between the ages of 35–65 from the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC)-Potsdam study (EPIC Centres - GERMANY, 2022).
evidence: This is a statement about the development of the GDRS model, supported by a citation.

claim: Barbara Di Camillo et al. reported in 2019 the development of three survival analysis models achieving area under the receiver operating curve (auROC) scores equal to 0.83, 0.87, and 0.90, outperforming the FINDRISC and Framingham scores.
source: Barbara Di Camillo et al. reported in 2019 the development of three survival analysis models using the following features: background and anthropometric information, routine laboratory tests, and results from an Oral Glucose Challenge Test (OGTT). The cohorts consisted of 8483 people from three large Finnish and Spanish datasets. They report achieving area under the receiver operating curve (auROC) scores equal to 0.83, 0.87, and 0.90, outperforming the FINDRISC and Framingham scores (Di Camillo et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Di Camillo et al., 2018.

claim: In 2021, Lara Lama et al. found that BMI, waist–hip ratio (WHR), age, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and a family history of diabetes were the most significant predictive features for T2D and prediabetes.
source: In 2021, Lara Lama et al. reported using a random forest classifier on 7949 participants from the greater Stockholm area to investigate the key features for predicting prediabetes and T2D onset. They found that BMI, waist–hip ratio (WHR), age, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and a family history of diabetes were the most significant predictive features for T2D and prediabetes (Lama et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lama et al., 2021.

claim: The models developed in this study are most relevant for the UK population aged 40–65 or for populations with similar characteristics.
source: Since we trained and evaluated our models using the UKB database, the models are therefore most relevant for the UK population aged 40–65 or for populations with similar characteristics (as presented in Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the training dataset.

claim: The UK Biobank observational study cohort includes 502,536 participants aged 40–69 recruited in the UK voluntarily from 2006 to 2010.
source: We analyzed UKB's observational data of 502,536 participants aged 40–69 recruited in the UK voluntarily from 2006 to 2010.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the UK Biobank cohort.

claim: Out of the UK Biobank cohort, 20,346 participants revisited the UKB assessment center from 2012 to 2013 for an additional medical assessment.
source: Out of this cohort, we used the data of 20,346 participants who revisited the UKB assessment center from 2012 to 2013 for an additional medical assessment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the subset of participants used in the study.

claim: 48,705 participants revisited for a second or third visit from 2014 onward for an imaging visit and underwent an additional, similar medical check.
source: We also used the data of 48,705 participants who revisited for a second or third visit from 2014 onward for an imaging visit and underwent an additional, similar medical check.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the subset of participants used in the study.

claim: Participants were screened to keep only those not being treated for nor having in the past T2D.
source: We screened the participants to keep only those not being treated for nor having in the past T2D.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the inclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Participants whose average blood sugar level for the past 2–3 months (hemoglobin A1c [HbA1c%]) was below 4% or above 6.5% were screened out.
source: We also screened out participants whose average blood sugar level for the past 2–3 months (hemoglobin A1c [HbA1c%]) was below 4% or above 6.5%.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the exclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Of the 44,709 participants in the study cohort, 1.79% developed T2D during a follow-up period of 7.3 ± 2.3 years.
source: Of the remaining 44,709 participants in our study cohort, 1.79% developed T2D during a follow-up period of 7.3 ± 2.3 years (Table 1, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the T2D incidence in the study cohort, supported by Table 1 and Figure 1A.

claim: 0.5% of participants reported being healthy with a median HbA1c% value of 6.7%, while the cutoff for having T2D is 6.5%.
source: For this estimate, we used the data from a subpopulation of our patients and found that 0.5% of participants reported being healthy with a median HbA1c% value of 6.7%, while the cutoff for having T2D is 6.5% (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the bias in self-reporting, supported by data analysis.

claim: The study used 41 PRSs with 129 ± 37.8 SNPs on average for each PRS.
source: We used 41 PRSs with 129 ± 37.8 SNPs on average for each PRS.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genetic data used in the study.

claim: After removing duplicate SNPs, 2267 SNPs remained for use in the models.
source: We also used the single SNPs of each PRS as some of the models' features; after removing duplicate SNPs, we remained with 2267 SNPs (see 'Genetic data').
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genetic data processing.

claim: The most predictive features of the anthropometry model are the WHR and BMI.
source: The WHR and BMI have the highest predictability in the anthropometric model (Figure 3D).
evidence: This statement is supported by Figure 3D showing feature importance.

claim: WHR and BMI are body habitus measures associated with chronic illness.
source: These two body habitus measures are indicators associated with chronic illness (Eckel et al., 2005; Cheng et al., 2010; Jafari-Koshki et al., 2016; Qiao and Nyamdorj, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to studies on body habitus and chronic illness.

claim: The HbA1c% feature had the highest predictive power in the four blood test model since it is one of the criteria for T2D diagnosis.
source: As expected, the HbA1c% feature had the highest predictive power since it is one of the criteria for T2D diagnosis.
evidence: This is a statement combining data observation with established medical knowledge.

claim: Age and sex had a low OR value in the four blood test model, meaning that they hardly contributed to the model, probably because of the T2D-relevant information of these features latent within the blood tests data.
source: Interestingly, age and sex had a low OR value, meaning that they hardly contributed to the model, probably because of the T2D-relevant information of these features latent within the blood tests data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the feature importance analysis.

claim: The prevalence of T2D onset within the normoglycemic group is only 0.8% versus a prevalence of 9.4% in the prediabetic group.
source: The prevalence of T2D onset within the normoglycemic group is only 0.8% versus a prevalence of 9.4% in the prediabetic group.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the T2D prevalence in stratified subgroups.

claim: The anthropometry model yielded an auROC of 0.81 (0.76–0.86) within the normoglycemic group with an APS of 0.04 (0.02–0.07).
source: The anthropometry model yielded an auROC of 0.81 (0.76–0.86) within the normoglycemic group with an APS of 0.04 (0.02–0.07).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model's performance in a stratified subgroup.

claim: When testing the models within the prediabetic group, the anthropometry model achieved an auROC of 0.73 (0.68–0.77) and an APS of 0.2 (0.15–0.26).
source: When testing the models within the prediabetic group, the anthropometry model achieved an auROC of 0.73 (0.68–0.77) and an APS of 0.2 (0.15–0.26).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model's performance in a stratified subgroup.

claim: For the normoglycemic HbA1c% range, the four blood test model yielded an auROC of 0.81 (0.76–0.85) and an APS of 0.03 (0.02–0.05).
source: For the normoglycemic HbA1c% range, the four blood test model yielded an auROC of 0.81 (0.76–0.85) and an APS of 0.03 (0.02–0.05).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model's performance in a stratified subgroup.

claim: The Clalit external cohort included 17,132 participants with a 4.1% T2D onset prevalence.
source: Applying our model to nondiabetic participants of the same age range population (see 'Mmethods'), the four blood test model achieved an auROC of 0.75 (95% CI 0.74–0.75) and an APS of 0.11 (95% CI 0.10–0.11) on a population of 17,132 participants with a 4.1% T2D onset prevalence.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the external validation cohort.

claim: In the Clalit normoglycemic population (N = 10,064 participants) with T2D onset prevalence of 2%, the model achieved an auROC of 0.69 (95% CI 0.66–0.69) and an APS of 0.04 (95% CI 0.04–0.05).
source: In the normoglycemic population (N = 10,064 participants) with T2D onset prevalence of 2%, the model achieved an auROC of 0.69 (95% CI 0.66–0.69) and an APS of 0.04 (95% CI 0.04–0.05).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model's performance on the external validation cohort.

claim: Within the Clalit prediabetes population (N = 7059) with a T2D onset prevalence of 7.1%, the model achieved an auROC of 0.68 (95% CI 0.67–0.69) and an APS of 0.12 (95% CI 0.12–0.13).
source: Within the prediabetes population (N = 7059) with a T2D onset prevalence of 7.1%, the model achieved an auROC of 0.68 (95% CI 0.67–0.69) and an APS of 0.12 (95% CI 0.12–0.13) (Table 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model's performance on the external validation cohort, supported by Table 5.

claim: The UK Biobank cohort suffers from 'healthy volunteer selection bias' and from 'attrition bias'.
source: While the UKB is a UK population-based prospective study suffering from 'healthy volunteer selection bias' and from 'attrition bias' (Fry et al., 2017; Hernán et al., 2004), the Clalit cohort is a retrospective cohort based on an Israeli population and suffers from ascertainment bias and diagnostic suspicion biases, as people with higher risk for T2D are sent to perform the related blood tests.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on bias in the UK Biobank.

claim: The Clalit cohort suffers from ascertainment bias and diagnostic suspicion biases, as people with higher risk for T2D are sent to perform the related blood tests.
source: While the UKB is a UK population-based prospective study suffering from 'healthy volunteer selection bias' and from 'attrition bias' (Fry et al., 2017; Hernán et al., 2004), the Clalit cohort is a retrospective cohort based on an Israeli population and suffers from ascertainment bias and diagnostic suspicion biases, as people with higher risk for T2D are sent to perform the related blood tests.
evidence: This is an inference about the biases in the Clalit cohort based on its retrospective nature.

claim: The study cohort's T2D prevalence was only 1.79%, while the general UK population's T2D prevalence is 6.3%, and 8% among adults aged 45–54 in the general UK population (2019).
source: Our cohort's T2D prevalence was only 1.79%, while the general UK population's T2D prevalence is 6.3%, and 8% among adults aged 45–54 in the general UK population (2019) (Diabetes UK).
evidence: This statement compares the study cohort's prevalence to the general UK population, supported by a citation to Diabetes UK.

claim: A 'healthy volunteer' selection bias reduces the T2D prevalence from 6% in the general UK population to 4.8% in the UKB population.
source: This bias is commonly reported as a 'healthy volunteer' selection bias (Fry et al., 2017; Hernán et al., 2004), which reduces the T2D prevalence from 6% in the general UK population to 4.8% in the UKB population.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on selection bias in the UK Biobank.

claim: An additional screening bias is caused by including only healthy participants on their first visit, which contributed to the reduced prevalence of T2D in the cohort of 1.79% T2D onset.
source: An additional screening bias is caused by including only healthy participants on their first visit. This contributed to the reduced prevalence of T2D in our cohort of 1.79% T2D onset.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of inclusion criteria on T2D prevalence.

claim: A healthy lifestyle and diet modifications are expected to reduce the probability of T2D onset.
source: As several studies have concluded (Knowler et al., 2002; Lindström et al., 2006; Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group, 2015), a healthy lifestyle and diet modifications are expected to reduce the probability of T2D onset; therefore, identifying people at risk for T2D is crucial.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to studies on diabetes prevention.

claim: The four blood test and anthropometric models outperformed the commonly used nonlaboratory models, the FINDRISC and the GDRS.
source: The four blood test and anthropometric models outperformed the commonly used nonlaboratory models, the FINDRISC and the GDRS.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the comparative performance metrics reported in the study.

claim: The models have the potential to improve millions of people's lives and reduce the economic burden on the medical system.
source: Thus, these models have the potential to improve millions of people's lives and reduce the economic burden on the medical system.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the models.

claim: The anthropometrics and the four blood tests survival analysis models achieved deciles prevalence OR of ×10.7 and ×42.9, respectively.
source: The anthropometrics and the four blood tests survival analysis models achieved deciles prevalence OR of ×10.7 and ×42.9, respectively, while the scorecard forms achieved OR of ×17.15 and ×47.7, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the models' performance metrics.

claim: The scorecard forms of the anthropometrics and four blood tests models achieved OR of ×17.15 and ×47.7, respectively.
source: The anthropometrics and the four blood tests survival analysis models achieved deciles prevalence OR of ×10.7 and ×42.9, respectively, while the scorecard forms achieved OR of ×17.15 and ×47.7, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the models' performance metrics.

claim: The anthropometry-based model retained its auROC performance of 0.81 (0.76–0.86) in the normoglycemic population but its performance worsened to 0.73 (0.68–0.77) in the prediabetes population.
source: The anthropometry-based model retained its auROC performance of 0.81 (0.76–0.86) in the normoglycemic population but its performance worsened to 0.73 (0.68–0.77) in the prediabetes population.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing the model's performance across stratified subgroups.

claim: Training a subcohort-specific model did not improve the results in stratified populations.
source: Training a subcohort-specific model did not improve these results.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of training subcohort-specific models.

claim: Applying the models to additional populations requires further research, and fine-tuning of the feature coefficients might be required.
source: Applying our models to additional populations requires further research, and fine-tuning of the feature coefficients might be required.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations and future directions of the research.

claim: The laboratory four blood test model for clinical use is highly predictive of T2D onset.
source: We assert that our models make a significant contribution to such identification in two ways: the laboratory four blood test model for clinical use is highly predictive of T2D onset, and the anthropometrics model, mainly in its scorecard form, is an easily accessible and accurate tool.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the performance metrics reported in the study.

claim: The anthropometrics model, mainly in its scorecard form, is an easily accessible and accurate tool.
source: We assert that our models make a significant contribution to such identification in two ways: the laboratory four blood test model for clinical use is highly predictive of T2D onset, and the anthropometrics model, mainly in its scorecard form, is an easily accessible and accurate tool.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the performance metrics and design of the model.

claim: The study used gradient boosting decision trees, survival analysis, and logistic regression methods to analyze the data.
source: We first analyzed the data using gradient boosting decision trees, survival analysis, and logistic regression methods.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methods used in the study.

claim: The study devised one nonlaboratory model accessible to the general population and one more precise yet simple model that utilizes laboratory tests.
source: We devised one nonlaboratory model accessible to the general population and one more precise yet simple model that utilizes laboratory tests.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the models developed in the study.

claim: Both models were simplified to an accessible scorecard form.
source: We simplified both models to an accessible scorecard form, tested the models on normoglycemic and prediabetes subcohorts, and compared the results to the results of the general cohort.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model development process.

claim: The models were tested on normoglycemic and prediabetes subcohorts.
source: We simplified both models to an accessible scorecard form, tested the models on normoglycemic and prediabetes subcohorts, and compared the results to the results of the general cohort.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the testing strategy used in the study.

claim: The Clalit database is considered one of the world's largest EHR databases.
source: The Clalit database holds electronic health records of over 11  million patients, dating back to 2002. It is considered one of the world's largest EHR databases (Artzi et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Artzi et al., 2020.

claim: Clalit is the largest Israeli healthcare organization, serving more than 4.4 million patients.
source: Clalit is the largest Israeli healthcare organization, serving more than 4.4 million patients (about half the population of Israel).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the Clalit healthcare organization.

claim: The Clalit database holds electronic health records of over 11 million patients, dating back to 2002.
source: The Clalit database holds electronic health records of over 11  million patients, dating back to 2002.

evidence: This is an inference about the impact of inclusion criteria on T2D prevalence.

evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies on diabetes prevention.
